criterion_notes.c1: No. The empirical study investigates internal operations, worker qualifications, water/effluent quality testing, equipment maintenance, and daily treatment volumes across 12 municipal water and wastewater treatment plants, rather than household or community water or sanitation service access. Municipal piped-water and flush-toilet rates (Table 1) and rural water-access disparities are cited only as secondary background context.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2, this study would pass Criterion 2 (yes) because it applies Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework to examine municipal treatment-plant institutional arrangements, roles, and regulatory compliance with SANS 241 water-quality testing standards. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, it fails Criterion 2 (no) because it examines internal plant technical protocols ('rules-in-use' such as rapid gravity sand filtration and backwashing), staff education/training gaps, inconsistent laboratory/in-plant parameter testing, equipment maintenance, load-shedding, and generic macro-level coordination issues rather than any rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, disconnection/enforcement, or access-governing regulatory structures). Note that plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the paper also fails Criteria 1 and 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Qualitative primary empirical study based on in-person semi-structured interviews with 18 employees across 12 water and wastewater treatment plants (WTW n = 10; WWTW n = 8), analyzed using deductive/thematic analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported empirical outcomes are plant-worker understanding of treatment techniques, worker educational/demographic profiles, consistency of in-plant water-quality parameter testing and effluent/water quality perceptions, equipment breakdowns, operator perceptions of whether plant treatment capacity suffices for daily plant load, and daily treated volumes (0.8 to 43 ML/day). No household or community access, connection, availability, continuity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is measured.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Within its own treatment-plant scope, the study identifies the population and unit of analysis (18 employees at 12 WTWs and WWTWs in Vhembe District Municipality), institutional/operational themes, plant-level operational and testing outcomes, and a qualitative semi-structured interview study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is published in English (interviews were conducted in English or TshiVenda and reported in English).

evidence_quotes.quote: This study aims to assess the institutional arrangements, operational challenges, and environmental concerns affecting water and wastewater treatment plants in the Vhembe District Municipality. To achieve this, the study examines the governance structures affecting plant operations, assesses the operational challenges such as infrastructure and capacity constraints, and explores the environmental issues impacting plant sustainability such as water quality.
Interviews were conducted with 18 employees (water treatment works (WTW) n = 10; wastewater treatment (WWTW) n = 8), including supervisors, chief process controllers, and process controllers.

The findings of the semi-structured interviews that were done with the supervisors and process controllers from 12 water and wastewater treatment plants in the Vhembe District Municipality were grouped into five key research themes: (1) understanding of water/wastewater treatment system, (2) educational and demographic profile, (3) water quality assessments, (4) operational performance and regulatory compliance, and (5) water volume in waterworks plants.

In this study, water and wastewater treatment plants serve as the action arena, where various actors engage to manage water resources. Chief process controllers, supervisors, process controllers, and operators are among the key actors that have been identified. The action situation covers tasks including managing plant capacity, sourcing water, and purifying water to meet required standards (Figure 1).
This reflects the “rules-in-use” of Ostrom’s framework within their organizational settings, indicating the established protocol and procedures governing treatment processes [26].

It was observed that workers are knowledgeable about treatment procedures; however, institutional issues like insufficient resources and poor institutional support affect the effective functioning of treatment plants.

raw_response.exposure: Internal treatment-plant institutional and operational arrangements (technical SOPs/'rules-in-use', worker educational qualifications and training, SANS 241 water-quality testing practices, equipment maintenance, resource/budgetary constraints, and electricity load-shedding)
raw_response.outcome: Treatment-plant worker knowledge of treatment processes, in-plant water/effluent quality parameter testing consistency and perceived water quality, equipment breakdowns, operator-perceived sufficiency of plant treatment capacity, and daily treated water/wastewater volumes (ML/day)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 18 employees (supervisors, chief process controllers, and process controllers) across 12 municipal plants (6 water treatment works and 6 sewage/wastewater treatment works) in Thulamela and Makhado Local Municipalities, Vhembe District Municipality, Limpopo Province
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E01: Wrong topic). Although the paper frames its analysis using Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework and mentions municipal water-access statistics as background context, the empirical study exclusively investigates internal water and wastewater treatment plant operations via interviews with 18 plant employees across 12 treatment works. It fails Criterion 1 (examines treatment-plant operations, worker qualifications, and water/effluent quality management rather than household or community water or sanitation service access), Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 rule-type scope (examines plant technical protocols, training gaps, inconsistent SANS 241 water-quality parameter testing, load-shedding, and maintenance shortfalls rather than rule-type mechanisms governing service access), and Criterion 4 (reports plant operational, water-quality testing, and daily treated volume outcomes rather than household or community access outcomes). Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it remains excluded for failing Criteria 1 and 4.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative semi-structured interview study with deductive thematic analysis
